Call centers: 12% don't track customer satisfaction at all

A customer who contacts a company almost never sticks to a single channel. They send an email, follow up by chat, and end up calling. To know whether they are satisfied, you need to look at their whole journey. That is far from the case in most contact centers.

A survey by CTI Forum and Liveops, published by Statista in 2025, asked call center managers how they evaluate customer satisfaction with their agents. The source does not state the exact year of data collection, so we present these figures as an order of magnitude published in 2025.

Three ways to measure, or not to measure

48% of respondents track satisfaction channel by channel: one indicator for phone, another for chat, another for email. 40% have an integrated measure across all channels. And 12% do not track customer satisfaction at all.

Adding up the two problematic situations, 60% of call centers have no overall view of their customers' satisfaction: either because they measure it in silos, or because they do not measure it.

Only four centers in ten can therefore answer a simple question: how did this customer's full journey go, across every channel?

Why per-channel tracking is not enough

Measuring channel by channel produces reassuring numbers that can hide a bad experience. A customer may rate chat highly because the agent was friendly, while being exasperated at having sent two unanswered emails beforehand.

Each channel, taken alone, seems to work. The problem is the sequence: repetition, waiting between contacts, having to explain the situation again. These pain points appear in no channel indicator, because they sit between channels.

Yet they are often what pushes a customer to leave. As we saw in another article, up to one customer in four leaves their provider because of customer service.

Customers do not think in channels; they think in problems they need to solve quickly.

And the 12% who measure nothing

Not measuring satisfaction does not mean lacking the means to do so. These centers have the same raw material as everyone else: call recordings, chat histories, emails, tickets. What is missing is the time or the tool to use them.

Classic satisfaction surveys also have limits: low response rates, a bias towards very happy or very unhappy customers, questions that are too general. Many managers give up on them for lack of useful results.

Finally, some of these centers consider that satisfaction can be inferred from other indicators, such as resolution rate or average handling time. Those measure efficiency, not how customers feel. A short call can leave a customer very unhappy.

Without any measure, these centers often learn about dissatisfaction only through escalations, public reviews or cancellations, in other words when it is already too late to fix the relationship.

Connecting channels through conversations

There is another way to evaluate satisfaction: start from what customers say, in every channel. Automatic language analysis reads call transcripts, chat logs and emails, and measures in each the tone, the emotion and the topic.

By linking these conversations to the same customer, you rebuild their journey and how their mood changes from one contact to the next. You can see which customers chase, whose tone is deteriorating, and which topics cause the most repeat contacts. Our call centers page explains this approach.

The models used are Mistral, BERT, Llama, GPT or Claude depending on the case; data stays hosted in France and is never used to train models.

Where to start

There is no need to overhaul everything at once. A first step is to gather one month of conversations on two channels, for example phone and email, and measure the share of customers who used both for the same problem. That number is often enough to show the value of a unified view.

From there, it becomes possible to track satisfaction across the entire journey, and to join the 40% of centers that really measure it the way customers experience it.

It also helps to involve agents. They live through the difficult conversations; showing them which topics generate the most frustration on the customer side helps them anticipate and route requests better.

What this means for you
